newsitem.title: USA: Group says privatizing Pa. liquor stores a loser.
newsitem.headline: Group says privatizing Pa. liquor stores a loser.

text.p: HARRISBURG, Pa., June 5 - A proposal to sell-off Pennsylvania's state-run liquor stores would raise prices and not generate much revenue for the state, a research group said Thursday.
Stephen Herzenberg, executive director of the Keystone Research Center, testified before the House Liquor Control Committee that a favorable analysis of the proposal by Price-Waterhouse was flawed.

Herzenberg said that the Price-Waterhouse study assumed that Pennsylvania would earn franchise fees significantly in excess of the fees West Virginia gained by privatizing its liquor operation. It also assumed that private retailers would mark up liquor prices less than is typical in other states.

"If you put these two assumptions together -- which Price-Waterhouse never did -- you discover that private retailers would lose hundreds of millions of dollars," Herzenberg said in a statement detailing his testimony.
Herzenberg said privatization under the Ridge Administration Plan is likely to yield much lower franchise fees than Price-Waterhouse predicts.

In addition, he said prices can be expected to increase because private franchisees will mark up prices at Pennsylvania's 757 stores more, not less, than in states with an unlimited number of outlets. Prices would be expected to rise most in rural areas.
"The bottom line is that there is no economic logic to privatization of state liquor stores from the perspective of the state or consumers," Herzenberg said.
